title: US Treasury Yields Near 5%: Why the AI Narrative Hasn't Broken Yet
dek: US money is getting more expensive, yet AI is still inflating while every other sector deflates. This contradiction either gets resolved by AI delivering a real breakthrough that pulls rates down, or by AI being falsified — but nobody dares slow down first.
why: Two institutional investors review Q3 global markets, focusing on the three-layer logic behind rising US Treasury yields and the AI prisoner's dilemma. The judgment leans cautious — suited to anyone trying to understand the relationship between the cost of capital and the AI narrative.
who: Investors and founders watching global macro and asset allocation, who want to understand the contradiction between rising US Treasury yields and the AI narrative.
skip: The Q4 asset ranking segment after 1:35:32 — the conclusions are fairly casual and can be skipped.

points.h: Q3 markets: the exhaustion comes from having no direction
points.body: In Q3 the S&P rose 2.1%, the Nasdaq was roughly flat, Japan and Korea fell 8-something and 18.5 respectively, the CSI 300 dropped 9.4, ChiNext fell 23 points, and the Hang Seng rose 8 points though Hang Seng Tech remained very weak. Commodities were the bright spot: WTI and Brent both rose 40 points over the quarter, and gold rose 8.5. But the host says his own feeling is ‘a strong sense of exhaustion’ — unlike the first half, when hearing a narrative and watching the market move still made you wonder what opportunity there was, whether to buy or sell, how to allocate. Now it's ‘tired, forget it.’ Ricky's summary: the first half was making money with your heart in your throat; this quarter was adjusting in total exhaustion.

points.h: Three forces driving US Treasury yields higher
points.body: A Clock Tower research note attributes the rise in US long-end yields to three forces: first, energy prices rising as the Middle East stalemate drags on and becomes long-term; second, resilient US nominal growth — Q2 real GDP growth of about 1.5 plus core PCE inflation of 3.4 adds up to 5% nominal growth, comparable to the late 1990s, when the combined level of US Treasury yields was around 5%; third, rapid expansion of corporate bond issuance as AI infrastructure buildout continues, and all of this against a backdrop of already-high US fiscal deficits. The remedies correspond to Middle East de-escalation, tighter macro policy, and a substantive slowdown in the AI investment cycle — but the latter two contradict each other.

points.h: Bond yields are credit pricing, not a buy-sell mismatch
points.body: Ricky explains it by going up a dimension: a bond yield is fundamentally the cost of funds generated on the basis of credit. After the Soviet failure in the late 1980s and early 1990s, the US entered a long period of low rates, because it was the most powerful country in the world and its borrowing cost should be the lowest in the world. Since 2018 the US has entered the mid-to-late phase of its national fortune cycle, facing more and more doubt, its credit downgraded, and so its borrowing cost must rise. In the two-dimensional world you see fewer buyers of Treasuries and more redeemers; in the three-dimensional world you see a decline in national power driving up borrowing costs. The US decision at the three-dimensional level is to keep pushing on AI, mobilising the whole country for AI buildout while also pushing manufacturing reshoring — which sets private capital and state capital competing for money, and everyone's borrowing cost rises.

points.h: Will AI infrastructure repeat the ROA trap of the great infrastructure buildout
points.body: Ricky compares US AI infrastructure to China's great infrastructure buildout starting in 2008: an economic entity dominated by CAPEX will inevitably see ROA decline — more and more assets, no breakthrough in production technology, so the return per unit of asset falls. When ROA drops below the borrowing cost, an asset crisis follows. The biggest worry now is that AI infrastructure will end up with ROA unable to cover the borrowing cost, while the borrowing cost is rising and the improvement in ROA is not yet obvious. David Weng adds: what's different this time is that deficits weren't this high before — past cycles didn't casually run into trillions the way they do now, and the current magnitude has gone beyond the range of human comprehension.

points.h: The prisoner's dilemma behind the calls to slow AI down
points.body: This week Dario wrote "We must pace the frontier," Musk reposted it saying he agreed, and Sam Altman also said in an interview that things should slow down, even saying OpenAI isn't in a hurry to IPO this year. A Reuters article on September 9 was titled "Researchers want AI to slow down, but labs can't afford to." Ricky sees it in three layers: first, right and wrong in the two-dimensional world cannot be overturned in the three-dimensional world — Asimov's Three Laws saw it a hundred years ago, and you can't stop a disaster before it happens; second, a unified alliance of three or more players is unachievable — the prisoner's dilemma ends with everyone choosing the worst outcome, and it needs an external force, which is government, but government only abandons its own problems once great-power competition produces enough damage and disaster; third, the funding side cannot tolerate such a long verification period — if within a year large models haven't proven they have a sufficient application and commercial environment, a lot of money will see runs and even broken funding chains, at a magnitude that would certainly be countless times that of the 2008 subprime crisis.

points.h: Large-model revenue of 150 billion against 200 billion of investment
points.body: Ricky does the math: across large models, revenue is 150 billion and investment is 200 billion. Split into frontier models and open-source models: frontier models bring in about 120 billion dollars of revenue on 100 billion of investment; open-source models take 100 billion of investment for 300 billion... no — 30 billion of revenue. Frontier model revenue alone is just that, and open-source models are still a long way from actually generating revenue to cover investment — not even profit covering investment. So whether these companies will still post big profit gains next year is under heavy pressure. More critical is the second layer: even if corporate earnings still rise by a small double-digit percentage next year, will the capital market accept it? Because the second derivative is actually heading down, and valuations are set on the second derivative, not on earnings growth. If you can't count white-collar replacement, you can't make the math work — and then it's definitely expensive.

points.h: Midterms: the probability Trump loses the House is very high
points.body: From BCA's research: over more than a century of US history, every midterm where performance on livelihood issues and inflation was poor, the probability of losing the House and Senate was almost 100%. The path laid out on the show early this year was that by June, if the US-Iran issue were resolved, energy costs brought under control, and Trump added some fiscal policy support, there was hope of holding the Senate. But neither of those has happened, so judging by the polls the probability Trump loses the House is very high — many swing states and minorities like Hispanics, once Trump supporters, are starting to switch to the Democrats. The probability Trump holds the Senate should be high. If he only holds one chamber of Congress, he becomes a lame duck.

points.h: A-share rally in Q4, but don't play too far to the left
points.body: Ricky thinks A-shares can still look forward to a rally in Q4, but it shouldn't be played too far to the left; watch mainly the volume of funds — if there's a short-term amplification in fund flows, it's worth participating. After that participation, switch to full defence and wait for the next, larger-magnitude breakout point, such as something clear on white-collar replacement, or clearer investment next year in the Huawei supply chain and the DeepSeek supply chain. If this rebound comes, it will certainly be led by tech, because many sectors have been tried without effect, and only tech can drive the market up. In Q3 most fund managers did no work and were busy writing self-criticism; in Q4 they'll have to work no matter what. David Weng is more conservative: still put cash first, second dividend low-volatility, third a narrower slice of tech such as the STAR 50, with a position of maybe two or three points.
